questions.author: Tacitus
questions.question: How does Tacitus make lines 1–11 (praefixa ... admixtum est) a striking piece of writing?
questions.instruction: You should refer both to the content and to the language of the passage.
passage: praefixa contis capita gestabantur inter signa cohortium iuxta aquilam legionis,
certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus qui occiderant, qui interfuerant, qui vere qui
falso ut pulchrum et memorabile facinus iactabant. plures quam centum viginti libellos
praemium exposcentium ob aliquam notabilem illa die operam Vitellius postea invenit,
omnesque conquiri et interfici iussit, non honori Galbae, sed tradito principibus more
munimentum ad praesens, in posterum ultionem.
Galbae corpus diu neglectum et licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum
dispensator Argius e prioribus servis humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis contexit.
caput per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque ante Patrobii tumulum (libertus is
Neronis punitus a Galba fuerat) postera demum die repertum et cremato iam corpori
admixtum est. hunc exitum habuit Servius Galba, tribus et septuaginta annis quinque

exemplars.question: 2022-4a
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Firstly, Tacitus makes this passage a striking piece of writing due to the army boasting about the killing of a man, which is extremely shocking, due to the profound permanence and sadness of death:
“certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus”
(with men showing their bloodied hands in competition).

This statement shocks the reader, since it is particularly striking how soldiers feel the need to show off that they have killed others, and even turning it into almost a game, comparing who has killed the most;
this is highlighted by the emphatic promotion of “certatim”.
The promotion of “cruentas” to before its noun, “manus”,
also portrays the extent of the violence,
while the sarcastic use of “pulchrum” in the next clause to describe the killing
shows Tacitus’ disapproval.
Vitellius, the next emperor, also found
“more than 120 letters of those demanding a reward on account of some notable deed on that day”
(plures quam centum viginti libellos praemium exposcentium ob aliquam notabilem illa die operam).

The multitude of 120 shows just how many men have committed the most serious crime possible, while the demand for a “praemium” shows how the soldiers are even proud of their murdering, which is shockingly disgraceful.
Tacitus also makes this passage striking by the gory account of Galba’s dead corpse:
“diu neglectum et licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum”
(neglected for a long time and abused with very many insults under the freedom of darkness).
The hyperbole of “diu”
conveys just how little care was taken over saving Galba’s corpse and keeping it intact,
while the violent nature of “vexatum” and superlative “plurimis”
highlights just how many gory wounds his body sustained – even after he had died, meaning people added unneeded attacks to his long-dead body.
Further abuse of his body is conveyed via
“cremato iam corpori admixtum est”
([his head] was added to his body – already burnt),
in which the promotion of “cremato” to before “corpori”
emphasises how his body has been set on fire, which is a striking and gory detail.
Even Galba’s head was abused, which is shown in the following:
“caput per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque”
(his head was fixed to a pole and mangled by camp-followers and attendants).
This quotation shows the extent of abuse Galba’s head sustained,
which is conveyed by the juxtaposition of the gory “suffixum” and “laceratum”
(the former again showing the boasting of the soldiers),
while the pleonasm of “lixas” and “calones”
shows just how many people abused Galba’s head in such a violent, shocking way.
Finally, this passage is made striking by Tacitus through his presentation of Galba’s fall from imperial power.
Despite being a former emperor, Vitellius (emperor after Otho) sought to avenge Galba and kill his assassins
“non honori Galbae”
(not for the honour of Galba).

This is particularly striking, due to the lack of respect shown by Vitellius to his predecessor, even if he was not the most successful emperor: we as a reader would still expect a certain amount of respect, which is clearly not the case,
due to the tersity and matter-of-fact nature of such an authorial comment.
Furthermore, the contrast between Galba being the most powerful figure in Rome, yet only being buried
“in a modest tomb in his private gardens”
(humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis),
is striking: this is such a rapid fall from power and honour.
The personification of the tomb being modest, as well as the promotion of “humili” and “privatis” to before their nouns,
conveys just how little public respect was shown at Galba’s burial, which is striking for an emperor who was even supported by the general population until recently.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). The candidate engages very well with how striking the passage is: directly answering the question is a hallmark of a top-level response. The point about the soldiers vying to show off their bloody hands has a good Latin quote, well translated, with excellent discussion not just about a literary device (promotion of certatim), but also in terms of how the candidate develops the point as it is striking that the soldiers almost turn their actions into a game.

exemplars.question: 2022-4a
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: In this passage, Tacitus tells of the events surrounding the murder of Galba. This passage is significant, as Galba is a key character in this book.
This is a striking piece of writing as visceral imagery is used to describe Galba’s burial, as well as many people claiming responsibility for his murder.
Firstly, Galba’s burial is described through the sentence
“Galbae corpus diu neglectum et licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum dispensator Argius e prioribus servis humili sepultura in privatis eius hortis contexit”

(The body of Galba, for a long time neglected and, in the freedom of the darkness, abused by very many indignities, did the steward Argius, one of his former slaves, cover him with a humble burial in his private gardens).
The lexical cluster of words of abuse such as “neglectum”, “licentia”, “tenebrarum”

is striking as Galba was the emperor of the state and despite his authority and status, he is treated in this way. What makes it more striking is that he is treated this way after death, and no one is showing Galba the respect that one often deserves after an untimely death.
His burial has a slight personal touch, as his ex-slave Argius covers his body, as no one else would do it.
Galba’s entire burial is bizarre, as it takes place in
“privatis eius hortis”
(his private gardens),

dissimilar to the funeral of another emperor. The reservedness and secrecy of Galba’s burial is striking as someone of his status is normally deserving of a larger, more respectful celebration of life.
It is clear through the smaller burial of Galba, people’s negative opinions of him.
Furthermore, this passage is striking through the way Galba’s body has been treated and the amount of people who are joyful in his death.
This is seen in the sentence
“caput per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque ante Patrobii tumulum postera demum die repertum et cremato iam corpori admixtum est”

(His head, strung up and lacerated by the camp-followers and the soldiers’ servants, before the temple of Patrobius, was at last on the following day found and was mixed in with his already cremated body).
Yet again, the visceral lexical choice of
“per lixas calonesque suffixum laceratumque”
creates dark and violent imagery in the readers’ heads, making this passage striking through its gore and disgust.
There is a lack of care for Galba as his head was
“postera demum die repertum”
(at last on the following day was found).
The unfinished participle “repertum”

displays how ‘unfinished’ Galba’s body was as his head was literally not attached to his body. This makes the passage striking and suspenseful as Galba does not receive the care and respect that an emperor should receive.
Finally, many people take pride and joy in Galba’s murder, as seen in the sentence

“praefixa contis capita gestabantur inter signa cohortium iuxta aquilam legionis, certatim ostentantibus cruentas manus qui occiderant, qui interfuerant, qui vere qui falso ut pulchrum et memorabile facinus iactabant”

(His head, attached to a pole, was carried about between the standards of the cohorts, equally between the eagle of the legion, while, in rivalry, they were showing their bloodstained hands, those who took part in the murder, who were there, who, genuinely or falsely, were bragging of their crime as something beautiful and memorable).
The multiple asyndetic balanced phrasing with the anaphora of “qui” in the phrase “qui occiderant ... facinus iactabant”

highlights the amount of people claiming to be there where Galba was killed, if they weren’t taking responsibility of the murder, making this passage striking as it is clear as how many people despised Galba and wanted him dead.

In conclusion, Tacitus makes this passage striking, mainly through the violent and visceral imagery used to describe Galba’s treatment after death and his burial. It is also striking as Tacitus reveals how many people are glad to see Galba dead.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4). The final point gives a long quotation which is well translated, and the candidate finds a literary device to discuss. Giving such a long translation without sufficient analysis limits this response to some extent: there is much that could be analysed in this portion to gain extra credit. A greater number of such analysed points could lead this response into Level 5.

exemplars.question: 2022-4a
exemplars.source: OCR, Exemplar candidate work, H443/03 Prose Literature (Tacitus), June 2022

segments.t: Tacitus makes this a striking piece of writing by describing horror of what has happened on that day.
“capita gestabantur inter signa cohortium”
(heads were raised between the standards of the cohorts)
which already creates a horrific image but to have them
“iuxta aquilam legionis”
(next to the legionary eagle)
creates a contrasts as the sign of the loyal soldiers, fighting for the good of Rome, is next to proof of brutal acts of violence.
The soldiers show off their
“cruentas manus”
(bloody hands)
which is more proof of the carnage that has taken place.
Tacitus also uses the repition of
“qui”
(those who)
to show the variety of things that happened which adds to the confusion of the day.
Tacitus shows the direct consequenses of these events.
The fact that
“plures quam centum viginti libellos”
(more than a hundred and twenty people)
expected a
“praemium”
(prize)
for their conduct on that day is chilling.
But Vitellius’ response of
“omnesque conquiri et interfici iussit”
(ordered them all to be found and killed)
is done for his own self-preservation,
“non honori Galbae”
(not to honour Galba).
The poor treatment of Galba’s body is also striking.
The body is
“licentia tenebrarum plurimis ludibriis vexatum”
(subjected to many liberties under the cover of darkness)
with the alliteration of ‘l’ linking the cover and the liberties.
Galba is buried in a
“humili”
(humble ceremony)
“in privatis eius hortis”
(in his private gardens)
by
“dispensator Argius e prioribus servis”
(the steward Argius out of his former servants)
which is not an appropriate burial for an emperor.
Galba’s head is also missing when he is buried and, in a twist of irony, is found by the tomb of Patrobius, who was punished under Galba.
The fact the head was
“cremato iam corpori admixtum est”
(mixed in with his now cremated body)
creates a pitiful image of Galba.

exemplars.commentary: There are some good points here (leading to Level 3), but the lack of range and the lack of development inhibit this response. It begins well with a good Latin quote about the decapitated heads on display. Explaining how this is shocking as the heads are next to the eagle is also a good development. The lack of development begins when the candidate then selects just cruentas manus for comment. There is probably enough background context to justify credit here, but it is always risky as often examiners cannot find the necessary context. This is definitely the case when the word qui is selected for comment. This is a fragmented and isolated word which is not contextualised, and so any literary point (repetition) is invalidated without the accompanying context.
